explorer.title: See where your system works hardest.
explorer.intro: Air is moving through the ducts in your walls right now. Tap a marker to see what goes wrong there, and the signs you can spot yourself.
explorer.alt: A drawing of a house cut open, with its furnace, ducts, vents, thermostat and outdoor unit
explorer.go: Not sure? Ask us to take a look

spots.label: Outdoor unit
spots.what: The outdoor unit pushes the heat from inside your house out into the yard. Dirt on its coil, a worn fan motor or a weak part inside make it struggle on the hottest days.
signs: The fan doesn't spin while the AC is on
Ice on the copper lines, even in summer

spots.label: Thermostat
spots.what: It tells the system when to run. Dead batteries, a spot in the afternoon sun or the wrong setting can make a good system look broken.
signs: The screen is blank or keeps resetting
The house never reaches the set temperature
The system turns on and off every few minutes

spots.label: Furnace & blower
spots.what: The furnace heats the air, and its blower moves air through the whole house, in summer too. The parts that light the flame wear out the most.
signs: It shuts off a few minutes after starting
A burning smell that lasts past the first run of the season

spots.label: Air filter
spots.what: Every bit of air passes through the filter. A clogged one chokes the airflow, so the system runs longer for less comfort.
signs: It looks grey, or you can't remember changing it
More dust on the furniture than usual

spots.label: Ducts
spots.what: The ducts carry the air to every room. Leaks and loose joints, often up in the attic, send air you've paid for into spaces you don't live in.
signs: Some rooms are always hotter or colder
Dust blowing out of the vents
Whistling or rattling in the ceiling

spots.label: Vents
spots.what: Where you feel the air. Blocked or closed vents upset the balance of the whole system, not just one room.
signs: Furniture or rugs over the vents
Little or no air from one vent
Damp or dark marks around a ceiling vent

title: What's your system
doing?
helper.intro: Pick the closest one. Here's what to check in the next five minutes, before you call.

items.label: No cool air
steps: Check the thermostat: set to Cool, and a few degrees below the room temperature. Replace its batteries if the screen is blank.
Look at the air filter. If it's grey and clogged, swap it for a clean one.
Check the breakers for the indoor and outdoor units. Reset a tripped one once; if it trips again, leave it off.
items.note: Ice on the copper lines or the indoor coil? Turn the cooling off and run just the fan, so it can thaw before we get there.

items.label: No heat
steps: Check the thermostat is on Heat and set above the room temperature.
Make sure the furnace's power switch is on. It looks like a light switch, on or near the furnace.
Check the filter and the breaker, the same as for cooling.
items.note: Smell gas? Don't touch any switches. Leave the house and call your gas company's emergency line from outside.

items.label: Strange noise or smell
steps: Banging, grinding or screeching: turn the system off at the thermostat, so a small problem doesn't become a big one.
A burning or electrical smell: switch it off at the breaker too.
A dusty smell on the first cold day is normal for a few minutes. If it lasts, call us.
items.note: Note when the noise happens: starting up, running or stopping. It helps us find the cause faster.

items.label: Water around the unit
steps: Turn the system off at the thermostat.
Soak up the water and move anything that could get damaged.
Look at the small drain line by the indoor unit. A clog there is the usual reason the water backs up.
items.note: Keep the water away from outlets, cords and the furnace's electrical parts.

title: Is your old AC
costing you?
energy_calc.intro: Slide to what cooling adds to your bill in summer, then pick when your system was put in.
energy_calc.label: Cooling, a month in summer
energy_calc.hint: Not sure? Take a summer bill and subtract a spring one.
energy_calc.source: A rough estimate, not a quote. Cooling costs fall as the SEER rating goes up. This assumes your system still works at the federal minimum it was built to (10 SEER before 2006, 13 from 2006, 14 in the South from 2015) and compares it with a new 16 SEER system. Your home, use and rates will change the result.

faq.q: The AC is running but the air isn't cold. What should I check?
faq.a: Make sure the thermostat is on Cool and set below the room temperature, then check the filter and the breaker for the outdoor unit. If the fan outside isn't spinning, turn the system off and call us.

faq.q: How often should I change the air filter?
faq.a: Look at it every month and change it at least every three months, more often with pets or a lot of dust. The Department of Energy says a clean filter can lower an air conditioner's energy use by 5 to 15 percent.

faq.q: When is it time for a new system?
faq.a: ENERGY STAR suggests looking at a new one when an air conditioner or heat pump is over 10 years old, or a furnace over 15, especially if it needs repairs often or the bills keep climbing.

faq.q: Should I repair it or replace it?
faq.a: It depends on the age, the repair and how hard the system works. We'll tell you the price of both and give you a straight answer. The choice is yours.

faq.q: Do you tell me the price before you start?
faq.a: Yes. Once we've found the problem we tell you what it will cost, and the work only starts when you agree.

faq.q: Why are some rooms always hotter than others?
faq.a: Leaky or undersized ducts, closed or blocked vents, or a room that gets the afternoon sun. A duct check usually finds the reason.
